newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rwanda says Zaire consolidating not falling apart.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda says Zaire consolidating not falling apart.

text.p: Rwanda's military strongman and vice-president Major-General Paul Kagame said that neighbouring Zaire, a third of which is now controlled by rebels, was not falling apart but rather was coming together.
"It has been said that Zaire is disintegrating. Personally, I see it more as the country consolidating," Kagame told Belgium's Le Soir newspaper in an interview published on Wednesday.
"It was a question of chaos which risked spreading to the whole region, now the contrary is happening," he added.

Zaire's ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko, in power since 1965, decreed on Tuesday a state of emergency across the whole of his sprawling central African nation in the face of the rebels' relentless advance.
Following Mobutu's declaration, security forces in Zaire's capital Kinshasa used on Wednesday tear gas to try and disperse supporters of the country's new prime minister, Etienne Tshisekedi.
Kagame said the progression of the rebel alliance, which is led by Laurent Kabila, was a "good thing for Zaire..., for Rwanda, for the whole region if not the continent."
Bordering on nine countries, Zaire had been a source of instability for nearly all its neighbours, he added.
"The change going on today is positive. The people of Zaire needed a change, (and) the region did too," Kagame said.
Asked whether he was ready to welcome back the 100,000 Rwandan refugees around Kisangani in eastern Zaire which the United Nations wanted to repatriate, Kagame said this posed no problem.
"All can return, but I am certain that some of them don't want to come back. They consider that it is not in their interests," he said.
"Some have already got to Kinshasa, members of the former (Rwandan) government, soldiers who fought alongside the Zairean army soldiers," he added.

Many of the Rwandan Hutu refugees, who fled their country three years ago after the victory of Tutsi rebels, are fearful of returning home because they could be blamed for Rwanda's 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
More than 90,000 Hutus are in detention in Rwanda accused of genocide and a handful have been sentenced to death.
